newsitem.title: USA: CS First Boston, Citibank to lead Venezuelan issue.
newsitem.headline: CS First Boston, Citibank to lead Venezuelan issue.

text.p: CS First Boston and Citibank have been named lead and co-lead, respectively, of a bond offering of an estimated $300 million to $400 million to be issued by Dupont energy unit Conoco and state-owned Petroleos de Venezuela unit Maraven, sources said Monday.
The issue would form part of a $1.3 billion package to finance a $2.2 billion joint venture between the two companies, dubbed Petrozuata, to upgrade Venezuelan extra-heavy crude.
The actual amount of the offering, which would be issued in the name of Petrozuata, will depend on the credit rating, a source close to the deal said.
"If it rates very well, the amount could be a substantial portion (of the $1.3 billion). If not, it could be near zero," he said.
"The goal is to get an investment grade rating," the source said, noting that such a rating would exceed Venezuela's sovereign ceiling.
An expected triple-B rating, for example, would correspond to an issue of between $300 million and $400 million, the source said.
"This is a well-structured project that should get an investment grade rating," the source said. "But this is just one piece of the financing.
The partners plan to meet with rating agencies Moody's, Standard & Poor's and Duff & Phelps in February.

They will subsequently meet with export credit agencies such as the U.S. Export-Import Bank, the World Bank's International Finance Corp (IFC) and the Overseas Private Investment Corp (OPIC), the source said.
The partners may also seek "more conventional bank borrowing," the source added. "We've got a lot of flexibility right now."

The Maraven-Conoco venture is the first of five proposed Venezuelan upgrading deals to reach the financing stage, and its success in raising capital would pave the way for the other deals to move forward, sources said.
Five banks were short-listed before CS First Boston and Citibank were selected and then approved by the Petrozuata board in Caracas late Friday, sources said.

Sources said many banks competed to underwrite the deal, not because the deal itself is particularly profitable, but because the winners could get preferential access to more attractive Venezuelan upstream projects in the future.

Petrozuata, a 50-50 venture, would produce about 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) of extra-heavy crude, or bitumen, from Venezuela's Orinoco Belt, and convert it into about 104,000 bpd of 21-gravity synthetic crude for export, Conoco officials said.
Drilling is slated to begin this year to recover 1.5 billion to 2.0 billion barrels of extra-heavy crude.
Maraven and Conoco inked their joint venture on November 10, 1995.
Venezuela's Orinoco Belt contains an estimated 270 billion barrels of recoverable crude reserves.
